before.content_html:
From Wood Pulp to Printed Page

Paper and board are among the oldest industrial materials, yet they remain central to modern design—from product packaging to architectural models. Both begin as wood pulp, produced either mechanically (grinding logs into fibres) or chemically (using reagents to dissolve lignin and release clean cellulose). Chemical pulp produces stronger, longer-lasting sheets; mechanical pulp is cheaper but yellows over time because lignin remains in the fibres.

Paper is measured in two ways. Grammage (gsm) describes mass per unit area. Copy paper is typically 80 gsm; a premium business card may be 350 gsm. Microns describe physical thickness: standard copy paper sits around 100 microns. The two figures usually move together, but coated papers can be heavier per micron than uncoated ones because the coating adds density without adding much bulk.

Key Fact

Paper weight is measured in gsm (grams per square metre); paper thickness is measured in microns. Standard copy paper is around 80 gsm and approximately 100 microns thick. Card and board start at roughly 200 gsm.

ISO Paper Sizes

The international standard for paper sizing is the ISO 216 series. The A-series is built on a single mathematical relationship: each size is exactly half the area of the one above it, and the aspect ratio remains constant at 1:√2 (approximately 1:1.414). This means an A3 sheet folded in half gives two A4 sheets, an A4 folded in half gives two A5 sheets, and so on. A0 has an area of exactly 1 m2. Designers use this relationship routinely when scaling artwork: an image laid out on A3 will reproduce correctly at A4 without distortion.

The B-series covers intermediate sizes (useful for posters and passports), and the C-series is used for envelopes (a C4 envelope holds an A4 sheet flat). In practice, the A-series is what designers, printers and students encounter daily.

The most commonly used A-series sizes in design and education:

SizeDimensions (mm)Typical use
A0841 × 1189Large posters, architectural drawings
A1594 × 841Exhibition posters, flip chart pads
A2420 × 594Technical drawings, display boards
A3297 × 420Design sheets, presentation boards
A4210 × 297Letters, standard printing
A5148 × 210Leaflets, notebooks
A6105 × 148Postcards, pocket notebooks

Types of Paper

Layout paper is thin and slightly translucent—ideal for developing ideas quickly in pencil. Designers layer sheets over earlier sketches to refine forms without starting from scratch. Tracing paper is more transparent still, used to copy existing drawings accurately. Cartridge paper is the general-purpose drawing paper used in most D&T studios: heavier than layout paper (typically 100–140 gsm), with a slightly textured surface that holds pencil and ink well. Bleed-proof paper has an extra smooth coating that stops alcohol-based markers bleeding through to the sheet beneath.

Recycled paper is made from post-consumer waste fibres that have been de-inked and re-pulped. Each recycling cycle shortens the fibres slightly, which reduces strength over successive cycles, but modern paper can contain 100% recycled content for many applications. Recycled paper typically has a slightly grey or cream tint rather than the bright white of virgin-fibre sheets, because optical brightening agents (OBAs) are harder to apply uniformly to recycled pulp.

Types of Board

Boards are heavier-duty sheets, generally above 200 gsm, produced by laminating multiple paper layers together or using a thicker single-ply process. The main boards used in GCSE D&T are:

  • Corrugated board—a sandwich of flat liners bonded to a fluted inner layer. The fluting creates a rigid structure that is surprisingly light. Used in protective transit packaging and models. Typically 3 mm to 5 mm thick but weighs far less than solid card of the same thickness.
  • Folding boxboard (FBB)—a multi-layer board with a white coated surface ideal for high-quality printing. Used in cereal boxes, medicine packets and cosmetic packaging. The inner layers may contain mechanical pulp to reduce cost, with a chemical-pulp surface layer for printability.
  • Mounting board—a thick, rigid board (1.5–3 mm) used to mount and present artwork or photographs. Available in many colours. Commonly used by designers to present rendered illustrations or to produce scale architectural models.
Key Fact

Corrugated board achieves rigidity through its fluted inner layer sandwiched between flat liners. Folding boxboard (FBB) is the standard for printed retail packaging. Mounting board is rigid presentation-quality board used to display artwork and build scale models.

Laminating and Finishing

Laminating applies a thin plastic film (typically polypropylene) to a printed sheet. Gloss laminate intensifies colour and reflects light; matt laminate reduces glare and gives a softer feel. Both significantly improve the product’s resistance to moisture, tearing and everyday handling. Laminating is common on book covers, loyalty cards and food packaging where the printed surface must survive repeated handling.

Other finishes include spot UV varnish (a glossy coating applied to specific areas only to create contrast), embossing (pressing a design into the board to create a raised surface) and foil blocking (applying a metallic foil under heat and pressure). Each adds cost and requires specialist equipment, but can significantly increase the perceived quality of a product.

The 12-mark extended response question asks you to demonstrate depth in ONE chosen material area. For papers and boards, top-band answers include: specific named paper or board types (not just “cardboard”), precise properties linked to application (e.g. folding boxboard’s coated surface enables high-quality litho printing for retail packaging), and at least one sustainability point (e.g. recycled content, biodegradable vs laminated boards at end of life). The weakest answers say “card is strong and light” without naming a specific board type or linking properties to a product context.

A strong Q6 paragraph on papers and boards might read: “Folding boxboard is used for cereal packaging because its multi-layer construction combines a smooth, coated outer surface for litho printing with mechanical-pulp inner layers that reduce cost. At end of life, unlaminated FBB is recyclable and biodegradable, making it preferable to plastics for mass-market retail packaging.” Note: three specific facts, a process link, and an environmental evaluation in one short paragraph.

glossary_terms.definition: Cellulose fibres extracted from wood or recycled waste and processed into sheets for writing, printing or packaging.
Grams per square metre — the standard measure of paper weight and thickness used across the industry.
A lightweight, semi-transparent paper used for overlaying and tracing design drawings.
Bonding a thin plastic film to a printed sheet to improve durability, water resistance and appearance.

before.exam_tip_html: In questions about papers and boards, always name the specific paper or board type rather than writing “paper” or “cardboard” — examiners reward precision. If a question asks about properties, link the property directly to a product application (for example: “corrugated board’s fluted structure gives rigidity for transit packaging without adding excessive weight”). For 6-mark and 12-mark questions, include at least one sustainability or end-of-life point, such as recyclability vs laminated boards, to access the highest marks. Remember: for the 12-mark Q6, answer ONE material area in depth — attempting more than one means only the first is marked.

before.content_html:
Timber in Design and Industry

Timber is one of the most versatile structural materials available to designers, and the most popular choice for the in-depth extended response question in the written exam. Understanding the difference between hardwoods, softwoods and manufactured boards—and knowing named examples of each—is essential. The distinction begins at the tree: hardwoods come from deciduous trees (broad-leaved, generally slow-growing), while softwoods come from coniferous trees (evergreen, needle-leaved, generally faster-growing).

Importantly, “hardwood” and “softwood” are botanical classifications, not descriptions of physical hardness. Balsa—which is famously soft to the touch—is technically a hardwood because it comes from a deciduous tree. Conversely, some conifers produce surprisingly dense timber.

Key Fact

Hardwoods come from deciduous (broad-leaved) trees; softwoods come from coniferous (needle-leaved) trees. The terms describe botanical classification, not physical hardness. Balsa is a hardwood despite being soft; some conifers produce dense timber.

Named Hardwoods

The following hardwoods are named in the specification and are likely to appear in exam questions:

  • Oak—a dense, strong hardwood with an attractive grain and excellent durability. Used in furniture, flooring, wine barrels and construction. Oak can be finished naturally or stained; it reacts with iron fixings (producing dark stains), so stainless or brass fixings are preferred.
  • Beech—a pale, fine-grained hardwood that is very hard and resistant to splitting. Commonly used in furniture (especially chair seats and legs), tool handles and children’s toys. Beech machines and sands very cleanly.
  • Mahogany—a medium-density tropical hardwood with a rich reddish-brown colour and an interlocking grain that resists warping. Traditional choice for furniture, interior joinery and boat building. Sustainability concerns exist around tropical hardwood sourcing; look for FSC-certified stock.
  • Balsa—extremely low density (as low as 100–200 kg/m3), making it the lightest commercial timber. Used for model making and structural cores in composite panels (e.g. wind turbine blades). Despite its softness, it has a high strength-to-weight ratio.
  • Jelutong—a fine-grained, uniform hardwood widely used in D&T education for model making and pattern carving. It is easy to cut, sand and shape accurately, making it ideal for producing prototypes and moulding patterns.

Named Softwoods

  • Scots pine—a widely available European softwood used for structural timber, joinery and furniture. It has a pale yellow colour with distinct resin pockets. Moderately strong and easy to work.
  • Western red cedar—a naturally durable softwood with high rot resistance due to its phenolic oils. Used for exterior cladding, garden furniture and roof shingles without needing chemical treatment. Has a distinctive reddish-brown colour and pleasant aroma.
  • Parana pine—a fine-grained softwood from South America, unusual in softwoods for being relatively knot-free. Used in high-quality interior joinery, staircases and shelving where a clean appearance is needed. Its limited availability has made it more expensive than other softwoods.
Key Fact

Western red cedar’s natural durability comes from its phenolic oils, not a chemical preservative treatment—making it an environmentally preferred choice for exterior use. Jelutong is the standard studio modelling timber in D&T because it machines and carves accurately.

Manufactured Boards

Manufactured boards are engineered sheet materials. They eliminate many of the defects of solid timber and are available in large, consistent sheets (typically 2440 × 1220 mm). Key types:

  • Plywood—layers of veneer bonded with adjacent grains at 90° to each other. This cross-grain construction gives high strength in all directions and resistance to splitting. Structural grades (e.g. WBP—water and boil proof) are used in construction; decorative grades use hardwood face veneers.
  • MDF (medium-density fibreboard)—fine wood fibres bonded with synthetic resin under heat and pressure. Produces a uniform, smooth surface with no grain, which takes paint and veneers extremely well. However, MDF is heavy, absorbs moisture at edges and cannot be used structurally where loads must be resisted.
  • Chipboard (particleboard)—compressed wood chips bonded with adhesive. Cheaper than MDF or plywood; commonly used in flat-pack furniture (often surfaced with a melamine laminate). Weak at the edges and screws do not hold as well as in solid timber.
  • Hardboard—a thin, dense sheet made from wood pulp fibres compressed under steam and heat. One face is smooth, the other textured. Used for drawer bases, backs of furniture and low-cost panels.

Natural timber contains inherent defects that affect quality and strength. Common defects include:

  • Knots—where branches once grew. Knots disrupt the grain, weaken the timber at that point and can shrink and fall out over time. Structural timber grades limit knot size and position.
  • Shrinkage and warping—timber continues to absorb and release moisture after felling. Uneven drying causes cupping (edges curl up), bowing (along the length) and twisting. Kiln-drying reduces but does not eliminate movement.
  • Shakes—cracks that run along the grain. Ring shakes follow the annual growth rings; star shakes radiate outward from the centre. Both weaken the board and may open further as the timber dries.
  • Fungal attack—wet rot and dry rot fungi degrade wood fibres if timber remains damp. Preservative treatment (e.g. pressure impregnation with copper-based compounds) is used for outdoor structural timber.

Manufactured boards overcome most of these defects because the manufacturing process eliminates directional grain dependence, large knots and growth-related stresses. This is a key advantage when selecting sheet material for flat furniture components.

Finishing timber protects it from moisture, UV light and physical wear, and enhances appearance. Common finishes include:

  • Varnish—a clear resin coating that cures to a hard, durable surface. Polyurethane varnish is water-resistant and tough, suitable for floors and furniture. Satin and gloss sheens are available.
  • Stain—penetrates the timber fibres to change colour without hiding grain. Oil-based stains are absorbed deeply; water-based stains raise the grain slightly but have lower VOC emissions.
  • Paint—fully opaque finish that hides grain. Requires a primer coat on bare wood to seal the surface and improve adhesion. Suitable for MDF (which does not have a visible grain) and exterior joinery.
  • Danish oil / linseed oil—penetrating oils that soak into the wood fibres, feeding the timber and giving a natural, low-sheen appearance. Often used on hardwoods where the grain is intended to be visible. Requires periodic reapplication.
before.exam_tip_html: Timbers and boards is consistently the most popular choice for Question 6, and the exam mark scheme rewards depth rather than breadth. Use specific names: “oak” not “hardwood”; “plywood” not “manufactured board”. Link each property to a product application: for example, “beech is used for chair seats because its hardness and fine grain resist scratching and machine cleanly for an accurate fit.” Include at least one manufactured board in your response to show range. For questions on defects, name the defect (knot, shake, fungal attack) rather than writing vaguely about ‘imperfections’. Sustainability answers must be specific: “FSC-certified mahogany ensures timber is sourced from sustainably managed forests” beats “use sustainable wood.”

When answering questions on metals, always use the precise property name (tensile strength, ductility, malleability) rather than vague terms like “strong” or “flexible.” For 6-mark and 12-mark questions, link each property to a specific product application—for example: “aluminium’s low density of 2.7 g/cm3 makes it suitable for aircraft fuselages where minimising mass is critical to fuel efficiency.” For corrosion protection questions, name the specific process (galvanising, powder coating, anodising) rather than just writing “paint it”—and explain the mechanism. For Q6 on metals, a strong response discusses at least two named metals, their working properties, stock forms, and one finish or processing method with a real product context.

before.content_html:
Polymers in the Modern World

Polymers are ubiquitous in modern product design—from food packaging to aircraft interiors. All polymers share the same fundamental structure: long molecular chains of repeated units called monomers. The critical distinction for designers and engineers is whether the polymer can be re-melted and reformed (thermoforming) or whether it permanently sets on first cure (thermosetting). This determines which manufacturing processes can be used and how the product performs under heat in service.

Thermoforming Polymers (Thermoplastics)

Thermoforming polymers (also called thermoplastics) soften when heated and become rigid again on cooling. This cycle can be repeated many times without degradation of the molecular chains. This makes them recyclable and processable by injection moulding, vacuum forming, blow moulding and extrusion. The most widely used thermoforming polymers are:

  • Polythene (polyethylene, PE)—available in two main grades. High-density polyethylene (HDPE) has a melting point of approximately 130°C and is stiff, hard and chemical-resistant. Used for milk bottles, bottle caps and pipes. Low-density polyethylene (LDPE) is softer and more flexible—used for plastic bags and squeeze bottles. Both are readily recyclable (HDPE is recycling code 2; LDPE is code 4).
  • Polypropylene (PP)—a tough, semi-rigid polymer with excellent chemical resistance and a high melting point (~160–170°C). Its “living hinge” property (thin sections can be flexed repeatedly without cracking) makes it ideal for flip-top bottle caps, food containers and battery cases. Lightweight: density approximately 0.9 g/cm3, which means it floats in water.
  • Polystyrene (PS)—in its standard form, a rigid, brittle, clear polymer used for CD cases and model kits. Expanded polystyrene (EPS) is the white foam used in packaging and disposable coffee cups. High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) blends rubber to improve toughness and is used for refrigerator liners and display models.
  • PVC (polyvinyl chloride)—one of the most versatile polymers: rigid PVC is used for window frames, guttering and drainage pipes; plasticised PVC (with added plasticisers to increase flexibility) is used for electrical cable insulation, flooring and inflatable products. PVC is durable and weather-resistant but raises environmental concerns because chlorine-based additives can form toxic compounds at end-of-life incineration.
Key Fact

Thermoforming polymers soften on heating and can be recycled—making them suitable for injection moulding and vacuum forming. HDPE melts at ~130°C; polypropylene at ~160–170°C. Polypropylene’s “living hinge” property (repeated flexing without cracking) is unique among common polymers.

Thermosetting Polymers

Thermosetting polymers undergo a permanent chemical change when first cured. Cross-links form between the molecular chains, creating a rigid three-dimensional network. Once set, they cannot be re-melted or recycled—heating them too strongly causes charring and degradation rather than softening. This makes them extremely heat-resistant in service, which is why they are used in electrical fittings, worktops and adhesives. The four named thermosets in the specification are:

  • Urea formaldehyde (UF)—a white or coloured rigid thermoset. Used for electrical fittings (plug casings, light switch covers) and white bottle caps. Good surface hardness and electrical insulation. Brittle compared with thermoplastics.
  • Melamine formaldehyde (MF)—harder and more heat- and stain-resistant than UF. Used to surface kitchen worktops (Formica is a trade name for MF-laminated board), crockery and the surfaces of MDF and chipboard in furniture. The high surface hardness resists scratching from utensils.
  • Polyester resin (PR)—a liquid that cures with a catalyst (usually MEKP). Used in fibreglass (GRP) boat hulls and car body repair. When reinforced with glass fibre it produces a composite with good strength-to-weight ratio. Low viscosity makes it easy to apply by hand lay-up or resin infusion.
  • Epoxy resin (ER)—a two-part system (resin + hardener) that cures to a very strong, chemical-resistant material. Used in high-performance composites (e.g. carbon fibre reinforced polymer in aerospace components), as a structural adhesive (Araldite is a consumer epoxy adhesive) and as a protective coating. Stronger and more versatile than polyester resin but significantly more expensive.
Key Fact

The four thermosetting polymers to know are: urea formaldehyde (UF) — electrical fittings; melamine formaldehyde (MF) — kitchen worktop surfaces; polyester resin (PR) — fibreglass boat hulls; epoxy resin (ER) — high-performance composites and structural adhesives. None can be recycled by re-melting.

A key exam skill is comparing the two polymer types directly. This table summarises the differences:

PropertyThermoformingThermosetting
Behaviour on heatingSoftens and can be reshapedChars/degrades; cannot be softened
Molecular structureLinear or branched chainsCross-linked 3D network
RecyclabilityRecyclable (re-melt)Not recyclable by heat
Heat resistance in serviceLimited by softening pointExcellent — used near heat sources
Typical processingInjection moulding, vacuum forming, extrusionCompression moulding, hand lay-up, casting with catalyst
ExamplePolypropylene (PP)Urea formaldehyde (UF)

Examiner data shows that very few students choose polymers as their Q6 material, and those who do often rely on generic statements like “plastics are lightweight and cheap.” Stronger answers go beyond the obvious “PET bottle” examples and demonstrate breadth:

  • Name two or more specific polymers with their full names (e.g. “polypropylene” not “plastic”).
  • Link properties to mechanism: “polypropylene’s living hinge property means thin sections can flex thousands of times without cracking—unlike most polymers—making it ideal for flip-top caps.”
  • Include a thermoset example: epoxy resin or melamine formaldehyde in a kitchen worktop context shows you know both categories.
  • Address sustainability: thermoforming polymers can be recycled by re-melting; thermosetting polymers cannot be melted and are more challenging to recover at end of life.
before.exam_tip_html: The most common error in polymer questions is confusing “thermoforming” and “thermosetting”—remember: thermoforming = can be re-formed with heat (like a wax candle); thermosetting = permanently set once cured (like a hard-boiled egg). For 12-mark Q6 responses on polymers, include specific names, specific properties with values where possible (e.g. HDPE melting point ~130°C), and at least one sustainability evaluation. Examiners flag that choosing polymers for Q6 is actually a chance to stand out—most students pick timber, so a well-prepared polymer answer impresses at the top band. Remember: answer only ONE Q6 in the exam.

before.content_html:
Where Fibres Come From

Every textile begins with a fibre. Fibres are classified by their origin: natural fibres come from animals, insects or plants; synthetic fibres are manufactured from petrochemical or cellulose-based polymers. Understanding the source of a fibre is the first step in predicting its properties—animal and insect fibres have a protein structure; plant fibres have a cellulose structure; synthetic fibres are engineered, which means their properties can be designed for a specific performance target.

Animal and Insect Fibres

Animal and insect fibres are protein-based. The primary animal fibres the specification names are:

  • Wool—from sheep. The microscopic scales on each wool fibre interlock when agitated in warm water, causing shrinkage and felting. Wool is naturally fire-resistant (it chars rather than melts and self-extinguishes), an excellent insulator, and absorbs up to 30% of its weight in moisture vapour before feeling wet. Used in knitwear, suits and blankets.
  • Cashmere—from the fine undercoat of Kashmiri goats. Exceptionally soft and lightweight, with superior insulating properties. Significantly more expensive than standard wool due to the small yield per animal (typically 150–200 g per goat per year). Used in luxury knitwear and scarves.
  • Mohair—from Angora goats. Long, lustrous, fine fibres with a silky appearance and high sheen. Resilient (springs back quickly) and durable compared with other luxury fibres. Used in high-end knitwear, suiting and upholstery.
  • Angora—from Angora rabbits (not goats; the name is shared but the animal differs). Extremely fine, lightweight and fluffy. Poorly resilient—the fibres tend to shed and pill with wear. Often blended with wool to improve durability while retaining softness.
  • Alpaca—from alpacas. Similar to wool in structure but lacks the irritating scales that cause wool to feel scratchy against sensitive skin. Hypoallergenic, warm and lustrous. Used in outdoor clothing and knitwear.
  • Silk—from the cocoon of the silkworm (Bombyx mori). The silkworm spins a continuous filament up to 900 metres long. Silk is strong, lustrous, naturally temperature-regulating (warm in cool conditions, cool in warm conditions) and extremely fine. Used in luxury clothing, ties and parachute fabric historically. High cost reflects the labour-intensive reeling process.
Key Fact

Silk comes from the continuous filament cocoon of the silkworm (Bombyx mori) and is one of the strongest natural fibres. Wool is naturally fire-resistant because its protein structure (keratin) chars rather than melts and self-extinguishes. Cashmere comes from the undercoat of Kashmiri goats.

Plant Fibres

Plant fibres are cellulose-based and include:

  • Cotton—from the seed pod of the cotton plant. The most widely used natural fibre globally. Soft, breathable and highly absorbent (can hold up to 27 times its weight in water). Cotton is easy to wash and dye. Weaknesses: low elasticity (it creases easily), shrinks in hot water, and conventional cotton farming uses large amounts of pesticides and water. Organic cotton addresses some environmental concerns.
  • Linen (flax)—from the stem of the flax plant. Stronger than cotton when wet, with low elasticity (prone to creasing). Naturally cool to the touch because of its high thermal conductivity. Used in summer clothing, tablecloths and bedding.
  • Hemp—from the cannabis plant stem. Very strong and durable with natural antibacterial properties. Requires minimal pesticides. Coarser than cotton but becoming increasingly popular in sustainable fashion as processing techniques improve.
  • Jute—a coarse plant fibre used for sacking, hessian and rope. Biodegradable and inexpensive, but low durability in comparison to other natural fibres.

Regenerated and Synthetic Fibres

Rayon / viscose—regenerated fibres made by dissolving cellulose (wood pulp) and extruding it through fine holes to form filaments. Viscose has a soft, silky feel and drapes well. It is not synthetic in the strict sense (the raw material is natural cellulose) but the manufacturing process is wholly industrial. Tencel (Lyocell) is a more environmentally responsible regenerated cellulose fibre—the closed-loop Lyocell process recovers over 99% of the solvent, making it significantly more sustainable than conventional viscose.

Fully synthetic fibres are manufactured from petrochemical polymers:

  • Polyester—the most widely used synthetic fibre. Strong, quick-drying, wrinkle-resistant and retains shape well. Low moisture absorption (dries quickly but may feel clammy in hot conditions). Used in outdoor clothing, sportswear and most woven fabrics in blended yarns.
  • Nylon—the first fully synthetic fibre. Extremely strong and abrasion-resistant. Used in hosiery, ropes, parachutes and sportswear. Low moisture absorption.
  • Acrylic—designed to mimic wool. Lightweight, warm and soft. Less expensive than wool; machine washable. Weaker wet strength and pills more readily than wool. Used in knitwear, fleece and craft yarn.
  • Elastane (Lycra)—a segmented polyurethane fibre with exceptional elasticity—it can stretch up to five times its resting length and fully recover. Always used blended (typically 2–20% in a fabric) because pure elastane fabric does not hold shape. Used in sportswear, swimwear and stretch denim.
  • Aramid—a high-performance synthetic (e.g. Kevlar and Nomex). Extremely high tensile strength and heat resistance. Used in body armour, fire-protective clothing and aerospace applications. Far more expensive than everyday synthetics.
  • Tactel—a branded form of nylon microfibre developed by Invista. Softer, lighter and more breathable than standard nylon. Used in sportswear, lingerie and outdoor technical clothing.
Key Fact

The specification names two branded fibres explicitly: Tactel is a branded nylon microfibre (softer and more breathable than standard nylon) used in sportswear; Tencel is a branded lyocell regenerated cellulose fibre produced in a closed-loop process that recovers 99%+ of solvent, making it highly sustainable.

A blended fibre mixes two or more different fibre types in the same yarn (e.g. 80% cotton / 20% polyester). A mixed fabric combines different yarns in the same weave (e.g. a cotton warp with a polyester weft). The difference matters for labelling and recycling—blended yarns are impossible to separate, making end-of-life fibre recovery very difficult.

Common blending rationale:

  • Cotton + polyester: cotton’s softness and breathability + polyester’s strength and wrinkle resistance. Standard in shirts and workwear.
  • Wool + acrylic: wool’s warmth and natural feel + acrylic’s lower cost and machine-washability. Common in affordable knitwear.
  • Angora + wool: angora’s extreme softness + wool’s durability (angora fibres shed readily on their own). Used in luxury knitwear.

Exam questions may ask you to compare fibre properties for a specific product. Properties to know:

PropertyHigh exampleLow example
StrengthNylon, silk, aramidAngora, cotton (wet)
ElasticityElastane (Lycra)Cotton, linen
AbsorbencyCotton (27× its weight), woolNylon, polyester
InsulationCashmere, woolCotton, linen (cool feel)
DurabilityNylon, polyester, aramidAngora, low-grade viscose
FlammabilityCotton (burns readily)Wool (self-extinguishes)
before.exam_tip_html: Questions on fibres often ask you to justify a material choice for a specific product. Always link the property to a product context—for example: “elastane is blended into swimwear at around 10% because it allows the fabric to stretch with the swimmer’s movements and fully recover its shape after each stroke, which polyester alone cannot achieve.” For questions on sustainability, name specific processes: Tencel’s closed-loop production and cotton’s pesticide intensity are both exam-relevant details. Avoid vague answers: “wool is natural so it’s sustainable” misses the fuller picture of land use and dyeing processes. For the 12-mark Q6 on fibres and textiles, include both a natural and a synthetic fibre with a comparison of their properties and at least one sustainability point.

lessons.title: Woven, Non-Woven and Knitted Textile Construction

before.exam_tip_html: For questions on fabric construction, always state the structural reason behind the property—don’t just say “plain weave is strong.” Instead: “plain weave has the greatest number of interlacement points of any weave structure, locking yarns firmly and giving high abrasion resistance.” If a question gives you a product (e.g. a denim jacket) and asks you to justify the fabric construction choice, identify the weave pattern (2/1 twill), explain its properties (diagonal rib, abrasion resistance, good drape) and link each to the product use. For non-wovens, remember felt does not fray—this is a distinct examiner-friendly fact. For 12-mark Q6 questions on fibres and textiles, you are expected to cover both fibre type and fabric construction—combining Lesson 5 and Lesson 6 content in your response will access the higher mark bands.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does plain weave have the highest durability of the three fundamental weaves?

Give one example of a twill-woven fabric used in everyday clothing.

before.content_html:
From Fibre to Fabric

Choosing the right fibre is only the beginning. The way fibres are assembled into a fabric structure determines how the final textile performs—its strength, drape, stretch, durability and appearance. Three major construction methods exist: weaving (interlacing two sets of yarns at right angles), knitting (looping a single yarn into interlocking stitches) and non-woven processes (bonding fibres directly into a sheet without spinning or weaving). Each gives a different combination of properties.

Woven Fabrics

Weaving interlaces two sets of yarn. The yarn running lengthways on the loom is the warp; the yarn running crossways (inserted by a shuttle or rapier on each pass) is the weft. The pattern of interlacing determines the weave structure. The three fundamental weaves are:

Plain weave is the most basic and most common construction. The weft passes over one warp thread and under the next, reversing on the following row. This produces a symmetrical, grid-like pattern that is the same on both sides. It has the most interlacement points of any weave, which gives it:

  • High durability—many interlacement points mean yarns are held firmly.
  • Low drape—the firm structure does not hang or flow easily.
  • Tendency to fray—cut edges must be finished or seamed.

Examples: cotton calico, muslin, taffeta, canvas. Used in shirts, bags, sails and base fabrics for printing.

Twill weave passes the weft over two (or more) warp threads before going under one, shifting by one thread on each row. This creates the characteristic diagonal rib line visible on the fabric surface. Properties:

  • Better drape than plain weave—fewer interlacement points allow yarns to move more freely.
  • Good abrasion resistance—the diagonal rib distributes friction across a larger yarn area.
  • Can be woven more tightly—so it can be heavier and more windproof than plain weave at the same yarn count.

Examples: denim (2/1 twill with indigo-dyed warp), herringbone, gabardine. Used in jeans, suits, uniforms and upholstery.

Satin weave has warp threads floating over four or more weft threads before interlacing. The very few interlacement points mean long yarn floats lie flat on the surface, creating the fabric’s characteristic smooth, high-sheen appearance. Properties:

  • Excellent drape—minimal interlacement allows the fabric to hang fluidly.
  • Lustrous surface—long yarn floats reflect light uniformly.
  • Snagging risk—long floating yarns catch easily on rough surfaces.
  • Distinct face and back—the two surfaces look very different.

Examples: silk satin, polyester satin, sateen (using cotton). Used in eveningwear, linings, bedding and parachute fabric.

Key Fact

Plain weave has the most interlacement points—making it the most durable but with the least drape. Twill weave has a diagonal rib; it drapes better and resists abrasion well (hence denim). Satin weave has long yarn floats creating a lustrous surface with excellent drape but a snagging risk.

Non-Woven Fabrics

Non-woven fabrics are produced without spinning or weaving. Fibres are laid as a web and bonded together by one of three methods: mechanical entanglement (needle-punching or hydroentangling), thermal bonding (melting a proportion of synthetic fibres to fuse the web) or chemical bonding (applying an adhesive binder).

  • Felt—produced by applying heat, moisture and mechanical pressure to wool or other protein fibres. The microscopic scales on wool fibres interlock and mat together permanently. Felt does not fray when cut (because there is no woven structure to unravel), making it easy to cut to shape for craft, padding, and industrial gaskets. However, it has low tensile strength compared with woven fabrics.
  • Bonded fabrics—include interfacing used in garment construction (fusible interfacing is bonded to the wrong side of a fabric with heat to add stiffness), geotextiles used in civil engineering for soil stabilisation and drainage, and medical non-wovens (disposable gowns, masks) where single-use hygiene is prioritised over durability.

Knitted Fabrics

Knitting uses a single yarn looped into interlocking stitches. The two main types are:

  • Weft knit—the yarn runs horizontally across the fabric. Stitches in a row interlock with those in the row below. Weft knit fabric stretches easily in both directions and is comfortable against skin. It also ladders—if a stitch breaks, the column can unravel downward. Used in T-shirts, underwear, socks and casual knitwear. Can be produced on circular or flat-bed knitting machines at high speed.
  • Warp knit—multiple yarns run simultaneously in the warp (lengthways) direction, each forming loops that interlock with adjacent yarns on each course. The fabric is much more stable dimensionally than weft knit—it does not ladder easily. Used in lingerie, swimwear linings, velvet backing and sports mesh. Generally produced on specialist Raschel or Tricot machines.
Key Fact

Weft knit runs the yarn horizontally; it stretches comfortably but can ladder if a stitch breaks. Warp knit uses multiple yarns running vertically and interlocking sideways; it is dimensionally stable and does not ladder, making it suitable for swimwear and lingerie linings.
